title: Effects of the surface on double surface Fermi arcs in a realistic tight-binding model of Na$_3$Bi (100)
authors: Vasilios K. Passias, Lucas K. Wagner
abstract: Na$_3$Bi is a topological Dirac semimetal (TDSM) that can support double surface Fermi arcs (DSFAs), which are important for its material classification and their potential use in spintronic devices. However, it is unclear how the surfaces affect realistic Na$_3$Bi (100) systems. To investigate the effects of diverse surfaces on DSFAs, we consider first principles derived tight-binding models of two Na$_3$Bi (100) terminations. On the stoichiometric termination, we find DSFAs as expected. On the non-stoichiometric structure there are DSFAs on one termination and two loops that retain many of the properties of DSFAs. Thus, the local properties such as spin momentum locking and hybridization with the Dirac points appear to be more robust than their global connectivity. That is, the surface can reshape the arc fingerprint without destroying the arc-like physics.
summary: This work investigates how surface termination affects the characteristic double surface Fermi arcs in the topological Dirac semimetal $	ext{Na}_3	ext{Bi} (100)$. Using tight-binding models derived from DFT, the authors compare stoichiometric and non-stoichiometric surfaces. They conclude that while the surface can significantly alter the global arc structure, the underlying local topological physics, such as spin-momentum locking, remains remarkably robust.
main_problem: The study investigates how different surface terminations (stoichiometric vs. non-stoichiometric) affect the double surface Fermi arcs (DSFAs) in the topological Dirac semimetal $	ext{Na}_3	ext{Bi} (100)$.
main_result: The local properties, such as spin momentum locking, appear robust, allowing the surface to reshape the arc fingerprint without destroying the arc-like physics, although the non-stoichiometric surface shows distinct changes compared to the stoichiometric one.
method: The research employs first principles derived tight-binding (TB) models, parameterized from Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, to simulate the electronic structure of slab geometries.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{Na}_3	ext{Bi} (100)$ surface, modeled using supercell slab structures derived from a 2-layer periodic unit cell. The analysis compares results from both charge compensated (CC, stoichiometric) and charge uncompensated (CU, non-stoichiometric) terminations.
key_observables: Double surface Fermi arcs (DSFAs), spin expectation value ($\langle \hat{S} angle$), electronic band structure evolution with thickness and chemical potential ($\mu$), and the presence/absence of cusps at projected Dirac points.
important_parameters: Surface termination type (CC vs. CU), film thickness (20 to 60 layers), and chemical potential ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The study assumes that surface charges are not large enough to materially change the Fermi level, and the TB model accuracy is assumed sufficient for the low-energy physics near the Fermi level.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic comparisons of Weyl vs. Dirac semimetals, the atomic structure of the two terminations, and detailed bandplots showing the evolution of Fermi arcs and bulk bands for both CC and CU terminations as a function of thickness and chemical potential.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical context of $	ext{Na}_3	ext{Bi}$ and DSFAs, details the methodology using DFT-derived TB models on slab geometries, and then presents comparative results analyzing the electronic structure differences between the stoichiometric (CC) and non-stoichiometric (CU) surfaces across varying thicknesses and chemical potentials.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter topology, the robust nature of local topological signatures (like spin-momentum locking) despite surface perturbations is relevant to understanding boundary conditions in quantum systems, which has parallels in open quantum systems theory.

In (a), we consider a time-reversal symmetry breaking Weyl semimetal with a minimum of two Weyl points having Chern number C = ±1. A Weyl point with positive (blue) Chern number is a source of Berry curvature field indicated by the outward arrows, whereas inward arrows denote a negative (red) Chern number Weyl point. The dashed Fermi arcs are on the lower surface Brillouin zones. The colored disks on the surface Brillouin zones are the surface projected bulk Weyl points. FIG. 3. Atomic structure of the two Na3Bi (100) surface terminations considered in this work. The green and blue atoms are the Na atoms, while the red atoms are Bi atoms. The red Bi atoms and blue Na atoms are in the honeycomb layers with bonds between them. The green Na atoms are between the honeycomb layers. We denote [010], [001], and [210] as the x-, y- and z-directions, respectively.

Fig. 3 shows the two surfaces we considered in this paper. One was the charge compensated (CC) system, in which both terminations have three Na atoms and one Bi atom, a stoichiometric arrangement. The other structure we term the charge uncompensated (CU) sys- tem, because unlike CC, CU’s terminations had a non- stoichiometric ratio of Na to Bi atoms, with the top ter- mination having one Bi atom and two Na atoms, whereas the bottom termination had only two Na atoms. Chemi- cally, we believe it is likely that CC is lower energy than CU.
